issues.title: AWG Router: AmneziaWG server panel with cascade routing and load balancing
issues.body:
I maintain AWG Router, an open-source (MIT) web panel for AmneziaWG servers: https://github.com/r-slashslash/AWG-Router

**Routing.** Clients can exit through other AWG servers or SOCKS5 proxies, chosen networks go direct, rules can be set per client and per domain. Domain rules work by redirecting TCP 80/443 to a local proxy that reads SNI/Host; QUIC is blocked for those clients, and ECH sites can't be matched. Each exit has its own routing table with an `unreachable` fallback, so when an exit is down traffic is dropped, not leaked. The tunnel is IPv4-only: clients get `::/0` and IPv6 is dropped inside.

**Panel exposure.** The panel lives under a secret path; everything outside it is minimal and answers with a generic `Server` header. The browser never contacts third-party hosts.

**SOCKS5 exit health.** A local Xray answers "connected" before it has reached the far side, so the check sends a TLS ClientHello after CONNECT and requires at least one byte back.

I'd welcome feedback, especially on fingerprinting and on how this behaves on real networks in Russia, Iran and China.

issues.title: Intermittent long delay (sometimes over a minute) on first packet after a LAN connection goes idle
issues.body:
I have two Linux machines on the same LAN, both running yggdrasil with multicast enabled. They discover each other instantly and everything works great - ping is around 2ms, HTTP works, no complaints.

The problem shows up after the connection has been idle for a while. If I don't send anything for a couple of minutes and then ping or curl the other machine, the first attempt is usually quick (around 20ms for the first packet, then back to 2ms), but every now and then it stalls badly - anywhere from 30 seconds to over a minute before traffic starts flowing. 
Once it gets going it's back to normal. It's a wired LAN with just two machines and a rock-solid link, so a minute-plus delay to get going again feels off and puts me off from migrating away from Tailscale.

A few things I noticed while poking at it:
- **yggdrasilctl getPeers** shows the peering staying up the entire time, even while idle. The link itself never drops.
- **yggdrasilctl getSessions** shows the session while there's traffic, but after about a minute of inactivity it disappears. I'm assuming that's the expected idle session timeout?
- **ping** seems to recover faster than curl

So my read is that the link stays up fine, but the session (and maybe the path/routing state) times out after about a minute of inactivity and has to be rebuilt, and sometimes that rebuild gets stuck for a long time instead of completing quickly like it usually does.

I spent some time reading the code to try to understand it, and I might be totally wrong, but my rough guess is that it's something in how the session/path gets re-established after going idle - possibly the two sides ending up briefly out of sync, where one side still thinks the session is alive while the other has already dropped it, and the recovery taking a while to converge. It might be down in the ironwood routing/session layer rather than yggdrasil itself, but honestly I'm not sure and don't want to point at the wrong thing.

Steps to reproduce:

- Two nodes on the same LAN, multicast peering, no manually configured peers.
- Confirm connectivity (ping, ~2ms).
- Leave it completely idle for 2–3 minutes.
- Ping or curl the other node again.
- Most of the time it's quick, but intermittently the first response takes 30s up to a minute or more.

Environment:
- yggdrasil version: 0.5.13
- OS: NixOS 26.05 on both machines

issues.title: XDRIVE: when the client disappears mid-download, the server uploads the rest of the response and keeps the session for minutes
issues.body:
### Integrity requirements

- [X] I have read all the comments in the issue template and ensured that this issue meet the requirements.
- [X] I confirm that I have read the documentation, understand the meaning of all the configuration items I wrote, and did not pile up seemingly useful options or default values.
- [X] I provided the complete config and logs, rather than just providing the truncated parts based on my own judgment.
- [X] I searched issues and did not find any similar issues.
- [X] The problem can be successfully reproduced in the latest Release

### Description

> 简述：在 v26.10.17（与 main 相同）中，如果 XDRIVE 客户端在下载中途消失（进程被杀或断网），服务端无法察觉：它会继续从目标读取，并把剩余的整个响应写入存储（复现中 20 秒内写入约 235 MiB、607 个对象）。这些对象要等服务端的 mux 子连接自行结束后才会被清理（约 2.7–13 分钟），期间该会话仍被持续 LIST 轮询。原因是 XDRIVE 既没有对端存活检测，也没有背压。

Version: v26.10.17 (`92ccc93`, the newest release and the same commit as current `main`), `network: "xdrive"`, `service: "local"`. XDRIVE is only in the pre-releases since v26.9.30; it is not in v26.3.27. The session logic involved does not depend on the backend, so remote backends behave the same way.

When an XDRIVE client disappears in the middle of a download (process killed, network lost, which is common for mobile clients), the server does not notice:

1. It keeps reading from the target and writes the whole remaining response into the storage. In the repro the client had received 22 MiB of a 256 MiB body; within 20 s after the client was killed the server wrote 246,869,084 bytes in 607 objects.
2. These objects stay until the server-side mux sub-connection ends on its own: about 2.7 min when the target closes the connection after the body, about 13 min with a keep-alive target. Meanwhile the dead session is still polled (about 2 LIST per second).
3. The server logs nothing after the client is gone, even at `debug`.

With a remote backend every abandoned download can upload hundreds of MiB into the storage account, consume API quota and leave the objects there for minutes.

If only the application connection is closed while the client stays alive (curl killed), the server stops writing within about 5 s and the folder is cleaned up, so the problem is specific to the peer disappearing.

| 256 MiB body at 16 MiB/s, `sessionTtlSeconds: 30` | storage at +30 s | +90 s | +180 s | server kept writing |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| download completes (control) | 0 B | 0 B | 0 B | no |
| client `kill -9` after ~2 s | 246,869,084 B / 607 objects | same | same | yes, the whole remaining body |
| client `SIGTERM` after ~2 s | 246,394,446 B / 515 objects | same | same | yes |
| curl killed, client alive | 0 B (one `.end`) | 0 B | 0 B | no, stopped within ~5 s |
| client `kill -9`, keep-alive target, watched 900 s | 246,453,796 B | same | same | yes; empty only at ~750–780 s |
| client `kill -9`, target sends `Connection: close` | 246,485,923 B | same | 0 B | yes; empty at ~165 s |

**Cause**

- `Listener.claim` marks the session active (`transport/internet/xdrive/xdrive.go:225`); the mark is removed only in the connection's `onClose` (`xdrive.go:234`). `collect()` skips active sessions (`xdrive.go:267-269`), so the folder of a dead session is not collected while the server-side connection is open.
- That connection is closed only when the inbound handler returns (`app/proxyman/inbound/worker.go:123-127`), i.e. after the server-side mux session ends. XDRIVE has no peer liveness signal: no heartbeat, no idle timeout. `Conn.receive` blocks on the reader channel (`conn.go:53-61`), `walReader.poll` returns quietly on an empty listing (`wal.go:295-297`), `holeTimeout` fires only when later segments exist (`wal.go:312-321`), EOF comes only from a `.end` object (`wal.go:365`).
- No backpressure: `walWriter.Write` appends to the buffer and `flushLocked` starts `go w.upload` (`wal.go:73-91`, `wal.go:127-156`); the semaphore in `upload` limits concurrent `Put`s, not unconsumed data (`wal.go:161-166`). Segments are deleted only by the peer's reader, so nothing limits what

issues.title: VLESS: Run client Mux directly on its transport
issues.body:
Let's use #7355 to fix write interruption in both client and server Mux. #7359 solves the same problem with a different wrapper and removes the MutexWriter this proposal uses.

For VLESS, keep pool configuration and selection in the existing outbound handler. When VLESS is selected, the Mux factory opens a direct connection and passes frames straight through the VLESS codec. This removes two intermediate pipes and their copy loops. Other protocols keep the current Mux path.

The direct connection also needs to stop XDrive writes. If the ring is full and a write is waiting for space, stopping the connection interrupts that write. During a normal close, the peer still receives EOF.

We tested VLESS Mux against stock Xray v26.11.9 and reproduced the XDrive shutdown case with a full ring on local test storage.

issues.title: Wait for log writers to close on shutdown
issues.body:
On Windows, an application that shuts down Xray and immediately renames its log file can get a sharing violation. `Close` signals the log worker, which releases the file later when it exits.

Wait for the worker to release the writer before returning from `Close`. Ignore messages received after shutdown and check for shutdown again when acquiring the worker permit. In `app/log`, detach both handlers before waiting so a worker can finish formatting a message that itself records a log. Keep `Start` and `Close` serialized.

The regressions hold a real file writer open during message formatting, rename the file as soon as `Close` returns, and check that a late message cannot create another writer. Both regressions fail on the previous implementation. The Windows run reproduces the sharing violation.

`Close` can now wait for in-flight formatting and writes to finish. The message queue remains best effort.

Windows and Linux each passed all 14 tests in `./common/log`, `./app/log`, and `./app/log/command`. The Linux run used `-race`. `go vet` passed for all three packages on both platforms, and the Windows main build passed.

AI-assisted implementation and tests.

issues.title: Geodata: Retain successful asset updates when another asset fails
issues.body:
When a scheduled GeoIP/GeoSite update loses a configured category in one asset, keep successful updates to the other asset. For example, a bad GeoSite release should not prevent fresh GeoIP data from remaining installed on disk and in live matchers, including after the next restart.

Apply each already-downloaded asset independently. Commit it if the existing registries reload successfully. Otherwise restore only that asset, reload the restored files, retain the error, and continue to later assets. This preserves successful updates in either configured asset order. Stop if a swap, file rollback, or recovery reload fails; a backup-cleanup error does not roll back an already accepted update.

Eight synthetic HTTPS regression cases cover missing GeoSite/GeoIP/both categories and successful updates, in both asset orders. They independently check each file and each live matcher. The four partial-success cases fail on the previously submitted implementation.

Validation:
- Windows Go 1.27.3: all 66 tests in `./app/geodata ./common/geodata` pass, with no skips; scoped `go vet` and main build pass.
- Linux Go 1.27.1 / CGO: the same 66 tests pass with `-race`, with no skips; scoped `go vet` and main build pass.
- Repository format check passes on the exact Git source archive.
- Existing tests use checksum-verified public CI GeoIP-lite/GeoSite assets from release 20261110012153; new update fixtures are synthetic and use a trusted local HTTPS test server.
- The full repository suite and macOS runtime were not run locally.

Downloads are still staged before any asset is changed. Recovery is per asset, including when a file is used by multiple registries; this does not promise per-registry partial acceptance of one shared file or global atomicity. The tradeoff is one full registry reload per accepted asset instead of one per bundle, plus recovery reloads for rejected updates.

Implemented and tested with Codex assistance.

issues.title: Fix noise after udphop
issues.body:
Fix noise emission when `noise` and `udphop` are used together.

Previously, noise state was keyed by the destination passed to `WriteTo`. udphop could replace that destination internally or switch the source socket without invalidating the noise state. Continuous outgoing traffic also refreshed the noise reset timeout, allowing repeated hops without another noise sequence.

**Implementation**

- Add shared `UDPPath` state through the existing finalmask dialer, containing the actual destination, a generation counter, and a mutex.
- Increment the generation after a successful hop changes the local endpoint, destination IP, or destination port.
- Have the noise wrapper clear its cached reset state when it observes a new generation. The next write emits noise before its payload, then resumes the existing reset behavior.
- Serialize the complete masked write against hopping, keeping all noise packets, configured delays, and the associated payload on the same socket and destination.

Generation tracking also handles returning to a previously used endpoint. Failed hops retain the active path and generation; attempts that leave the endpoints unchanged do not trigger additional noise.

Both configured noise items and Lua scripts use the existing emission code. Mask ordering, socket deadline propagation, receive handling, and connection cleanup remain unchanged. The existing connection stays in place, preserving Hysteria continuity. No configuration fields are added.

**Regression coverage**

- Source-port-only, destination-port-only, destination-IP-only, and combined changes.
- Continuous traffic, repeated writes on one path, and returning to a previous endpoint.
- Unchanged endpoints and failed hops.
- Concurrent hopping during delayed noise emission.
- Configured items and Lua scripts, mask ordering, reset behavior, deadline propagation, and socket cleanup.

**Verification**

- Focused noise/udphop tests and race detection passed.
- Finalmask and Hysteria package checks passed in short mode.
- GitHub’s formatting/protobuf check passed after applying the repository formatter.
- The full package run timed out in the separate Sudoku end-to-end harness; that run did not complete.

issues.title: XHTTP client: Add `scMaxPostRetries` to resend failed packet-up uploads
issues.body:
## Why

With packet-up the client closes the whole connection on the first upload that fails. Behind a CDN some uploads fail at the CDN itself. With Yandex Cloud CDN about 2% of requests got a 504 after the CDN waited 5 seconds for the origin, and some got a 502. So a long upload through such a CDN rarely survives. In our tests 3 of 10 uploads up to 3 MB broke with the current client and all 10 went through with resending. On a CDN emulator that checks integrity it was 12 of 12 against 4 of 12.

## What changed

- New client option `scMaxPostRetries`, 0 by default. Above 0, a packet that is not answered with 200 is sent again up to `scMaxPostRetries` times before the connection is closed as it is today.
- A 504 from a CDN comes only after several seconds. So one more copy is sent when the last copy was fully written but got no answer in 2 seconds. The first 200 wins and the other copies are cancelled. A packet with no 200 in 30 seconds fails the connection.
- The server gives up once it holds more than `scMaxBufferedPosts` packets after a missing seq. So with resending on, seq N is sent only after seq N minus `scMaxBufferedPosts`/2 is answered.
- `PostPacket` now uses the context it is given. The normal path detaches it from the connection as before, and the resend path uses it to cancel copies that are no longer needed. A cancelled copy no longer marks the HTTP/2 client as closed, otherwise each resend would open a new connection.
- With `scMaxPostRetries` at 0 the upload loop works as before.

## Why it is off by default

A resent packet may reach the server twice, for example when the CDN delivered it and then timed out waiting for the answer. A server without #7370 may read that copy again and corrupt the stream, and the client cannot tell which server it talks to. So resending stays off unless the server is known to drop duplicates. It could become the default some releases later.

## Testing and limits

- New `Test_PacketUpRetriesFailedPost` puts an HTTP/2 proxy in front of the server that answers 502 to the first upload of seq 1. The echo goes through with `scMaxPostRetries` 2 and times out with 0.
- `go test ./transport/internet/splithttp/... ./infra/conf/...` passes, also with `-race`.
- Together with #7370 I also ran a proxy that forwards every third upload to the server and still answers 504, so duplicates do reach the server. The stream stays intact.
- Only packet-up. A stream-up or stream-one upload is one long request, and the client cannot know how much of it the server got.
- It does not help when the CDN fails the download GET.
- HTTP/1.1 `PostPacket` does not read the answer status, so there only failed writes are resent. The browser dialer has no write callback, so it only resends on errors.
- The extra copy after 2 seconds assumes the server answers soon after the body is written. On a slow uplink with large `scMaxEachPostBytes` the body may still sit in the socket buffer, and a copy is sent for nothing. Behind a CDN small posts are the norm, so this should be rare. 2 and 30 seconds are constants.

issues.title: XHTTP server: Drop resent packet-up uploads instead of reading them again
issues.body:
## Why

A packet-up upload can reach the server twice if a client resends it, for example after a CDN answered 502 or 504 to a request that did get through. The server already drops a copy of a seq it has fully read. It does not handle a copy that is in the queue while the first one is only partly read. `uploadQueue` pushes the unread rest of a packet back into the heap with the same seq, so the next `Read` may pop the full second copy and return it from the start. The stream is then silently corrupted.

Current clients never resend, so this does not happen today. The client side is a separate PR, and this one makes it safe.

## What changed

- The unread rest of a packet is kept in `uploadQueue.partial` instead of going back to the heap, and `nextSeq` moves on as soon as the packet starts being read.
- Any other copy of that seq is then below `nextSeq` and is dropped by the existing check.

## Testing and limits

- New `Test_UploadQueueDropsDuplicateSeq` pushes seq 1 twice before seq 0 and reads with an 8 KiB buffer. On main it fails with a corrupted stream, with this change it passes.
- `go test ./transport/internet/splithttp/... ./infra/conf/...` passes, also with `-race`.
- Nothing changes for clients that do not resend.
- A copy that arrives before its seq is read still takes a place in the reorder heap and counts towards `scMaxBufferedPosts`.

issues.title: panic: slice bounds out of range [8192:8171] in XtlsPadding (VLESS outbound, Reality + Vision), recurring ~6x/hour on 25.6.8 / 25.9.5 / 25.12.8
issues.body:
## Summary

A relay node (Xray terminates several inbounds and forwards everything through ONE VLESS+Reality+`xtls-rprx-vision` outbound to another Xray) crashes the whole process several times per hour with a negative-length `Extend` in `proxy.XtlsPadding`. All inbounds are dropped on every crash (about 1 s with `RestartSec=1`).

No `testseed` anywhere in the config (so this is not #5961's "invalid testseed" case). No mux: 0 `v1.mux.cool` connections in the log over 24 h.

## Panic (identical every time, only goroutine ids differ)

```
panic: runtime error: slice bounds out of range [8192:8171]

goroutine 640 [running]:
github.com/xtls/xray-core/common/buf.(*Buffer).Extend(...)
        github.com/xtls/xray-core/common/buf/buffer.go:153
github.com/xtls/xray-core/proxy.XtlsPadding(0xc00021f740, 0x0, 0xc0002e1a28, 0x1?, {0x19a0058, 0xc000254730}, {0xc000269200?, 0xc000730000?, 0xc00033fb40?})
        github.com/xtls/xray-core/proxy/proxy.go:519 +0x79e
github.com/xtls/xray-core/proxy.(*VisionWriter).WriteMultiBuffer(0xc0002e19e0, {0xc00047ea98, 0x1, 0x1})
        github.com/xtls/xray-core/proxy/proxy.go:390 +0x5dd
github.com/xtls/xray-core/common/buf.copyInternal(...)
        github.com/xtls/xray-core/common/buf/copy.go:99 +0x15a
github.com/xtls/xray-core/common/buf.Copy(...)
        github.com/xtls/xray-core/common/buf/copy.go:116
github.com/xtls/xray-core/proxy/vless/outbound.(*Handler).Process.func4()
        github.com/xtls/xray-core/proxy/vless/outbound/outbound.go:360 +0xc79
```

(v25.12.8, go1.25.5, linux/amd64, kernel 6.8, 1 vCPU. `Process.func3` on 25.6.8 — same frames.)

## Analysis

The high bound `8171` is exactly `buf.Size - 21`. In `XtlsPadding`:

```go
if paddingLen > buf.Size-21-contentLen {
    paddingLen = buf.Size - 21 - contentLen
}
...
newbuffer.Extend(paddingLen)
```

`[8192:8171]` means `newbuffer.end == 8192` and `paddingLen == -21`, i.e. `contentLen == 8192`: a full 8192-byte block reached `XtlsPadding` unsplit. `Extend` has no check for negative `n`, so `b.v[b.end:end]` panics with low > high (the `end > len` check only guards the upper side).

`ReshapeMultiBuffer` is supposed to prevent this (it splits every block with `Len() >= buf.Size-21`), and `VisionWriter.WriteMultiBuffer` calls it right before the loop, so a full block should not get through. I could not find the path by reading the code (`XtlsPadding` and `ReshapeMultiBuffer` are byte-identical in v25.12.8 and v26.11.9). Possibilities I could not exclude: a buffer that is mutated/re-used between `ReshapeMultiBuffer` and `XtlsPadding` (pool double-release?), or a block larger than `buf.Size` entering through a non-standard reader.

Cheap hardening regardless of root cause: clamp `paddingLen` at 0 (`if paddingLen < 0 { paddingLen = 0 }`) and/or reject `n < 0` in `Buffer.Extend`. That would turn a process-wide crash into a (harmless) missing padding. Note that `newbuffer.Write(b.Bytes())` also silently truncates if `contentLen + 21 > 8192`, so the root cause is worth fixing too.

## Environment / what was tried

- Topology: several inbounds (Reality-TCP-Vision, Reality-TCP-Vision with self-steal dest, XHTTP+TLS, gRPC+TLS) → one VLESS+Reality+Vision outbound → Xray 25.6.8 server.
- Panics occur with users of ALL four inbounds (so not specific to one inbound transport).
- Versions tried as the relay: 25.6.8 (~1 panic / 5–10 min), 25.9.5 (2 in 1h20m), 25.12.8 (~6 / hour, 434 in 3 days, clustered: up to 5 within a minute). Not yet tried: 26.x on this node (26.10.31/26.11.9 server side breaks sing-box Reality clients in our tests, so we cannot deploy it for production users).
- Config has no `testseed`; `flow: xtls-rprx-vision` only.
- Related: #2651 (same signature, fixed in 2023), #5961 (same signature on 26.2.6/26.3.27, closed with "don't set testseed"), #6072.

## Expected

No process-wide panic on any input to the Vision writer.

issues.title: FinalMask: Report TCP test write errors instead of hanging
issues.body:
### Problem

`mustSendRecvTcp` in `transport/internet/finalmask/tcp_test.go` calls `t.Fatal` from the writer goroutine, which `go vet` flags:

```
tcp_test.go:30: call to (*T).Fatal from a non-test goroutine
```

`t.Fatal` ends that goroutine via `runtime.Goexit`, so `close(waitCh)` never runs and the helper's final `<-waitCh` blocks until the package test timeout, losing the write error with it. The helper is also called with a zero-length message, where `io.ReadFull(to, buf[:0])` returns immediately, so nothing on the read side masks a failing write.

### Fix

Send the error over `waitCh`, which is already declared `chan error`, and check it on the test goroutine. The channel is buffered so the writer still cannot block, matching the previous `close`. This is the pattern already used by `TestTCPcustomClientRejectsMismatchedServerSequence` and `TestTCPWrapListenerRejectsImmediateWrapErrors` in this file.

`mustSendRecv` in `udp_test.go` and `mustSendRecvUDP` in `header/custom/state_test.go` use `t.Error`, which is safe from a goroutine, so they are unchanged.

### Verification

Forcing a write failure in the helper hangs the package for the full timeout before this change, and fails in 0.00s with the error after it. `go vet ./...` no longer reports the finding, and the package passes under `-race` and at `-count=30`.

issues.title: Sockopt: Report the real ioctl error from OriginalDst on Darwin
issues.body:
### Problem

`OriginalDst` in `transport/internet/sockopt_darwin.go` reports success when the `DIOCNATLOOK` ioctl fails:

```go
if _, _, errno := syscall.Syscall(syscall.SYS_IOCTL, fd, DIOCNATLOOK, uintptr(unsafe.Pointer(&nl))); errno != 0 {
	return net.IP{}, -1, os.NewSyscallError("ioctl", err)
}
```

`err` is the `os.Open("/dev/pf")` result from the top of the function, which already returned early if it was non-nil, so `err` is always `nil` here — and `os.NewSyscallError` returns `nil` for a nil error. The `errno` the ioctl returned is dropped.

Both callers (`tcp.GetOriginalDestination`, `udp.RetrieveOriginalDest`) only test `err != nil`, so they build a destination from the zero IP and port `-1`: `net.IPAddress(net.IP{})` returns a nil `Address`, `net.Port(-1)` wraps to 65535, and `IsValid()` does not catch it since it only checks `Network != Network_Unknown`.

### Fix

Report `errno`. It is already the branch condition, so the error is always non-nil.

### Notes

issues.title: Hysteria inbound: Close a removed user's connections
Hysteria inbound: Fix `RemoveUser` not taking effect on authenticated connections
issues.body:
A Hysteria client authenticates once per QUIC connection. After `RemoveUser` the user is gone from the validator, but a connection that is already authenticated keeps opening new TCP streams and UDP sessions, so the removal does nothing until the client reconnects. With keepalive that can be hours.

The official server can drop such a client through `TrafficLogger` (`LogTraffic` returning false, which is what `/kick` uses). There is no counterpart for it here, while the WireGuard and MASQUE inbounds already end the session in `RemoveUser`.

This checks the user again when a stream or a UDP session is opened and closes the connection if the user has been removed. The client reconnects and fails auth. Connections authenticated by the transport `auth` (no `clients`) are not affected.

Tested on v26.11.9 with two users and `xray api rmu` / `adu`: before, the removed user keeps working over TCP and UDP; with this, its connection is closed on the next request, the other user is not affected, and it works again after being re-added.

issues.title: [Feature Request / Proposal] Preventing IP leaks during core restarts / profile switching with autoSystemWfpBlockLeak
issues.body:
Hello Xray-core maintainers and contributors!

First of all, thank you for the recent work on native Windows TUN. Moving leak protection directly into Xray via WFP is a huge step forward and allows GUI clients (like v2rayN) to rely entirely on native Xray TUN rather than legacy multi-core workarounds.

I would like to ask for your thoughts on an architectural edge case related to how GUI clients manage the `xray.exe` lifecycle, and whether addressing it within Xray-core aligns with your vision.

### The Scenario
When a user switches servers, updates routing/DNS profiles, or clicks "Restart Service" in a GUI client like v2rayN, the client terminates the current `xray.exe` process and spawns a new one.

Because the current WFP rules created by `autoSystemWfpBlockLeak` are tied to the dynamic WFP session (`FWPM_SESSION_FLAG_DYNAMIC`) of the running `xray.exe` process, the moment the old process exits, Windows immediately tears down the `xray_tun` adapter and removes the WFP filters. For the ~1–2 seconds it takes for the new `xray.exe` instance to initialize Wintun and re-apply `autoSystemRoutingTable` / `autoSystemWfpBlockLeak`, the OS falls back to the physical interface (direct), causing a brief IP/traffic leak.

### Possible Approaches
I am wondering what the maintainers think about bridging this restart gap natively in Xray. A couple of concepts come to mind:

1. **CLI-Managed / Companion WFP Lock:**
   Adding an optional flag or lightweight CLI subcommand (e.g., `xray tun-wfp lock` / `unlock`, or a helper mode bound to the parent GUI PID so it still utilizes `FWPM_SESSION_FLAG_DYNAMIC` for crash safety) that holds the baseline `"all"` / `"allexceptlan"` WFP block rules across worker restarts. This way, a GUI client could arm the WFP filter once when starting its session, restart `xray.exe` processes freely without dropping the WFP wall during the 1–2s gap, and disarm it on deliberate exit.

2. **Graceful Config Reloading for TUN:**
   While Xray already has gRPC APIs for dynamic outbound/routing updates, full profile switches in GUI clients often rewrite the entire config. Allowing `xray.exe` to reload its configuration on the fly (via API or signal) without destroying the active `wintun` adapter and its dynamic WFP session would eliminate both the Wintun recreation delay and the leak window.

### Question to Maintainers
How do you view this problem from Xray's design perspective?
1. Do you think bridging this restart gap belongs with in Xray-core, or do you consider it strictly the responsibility of external GUI clients?
2. If addressing it in Xray-core makes sense to you, what architectural direction would you prefer (one of the concepts above, or a completely different approach)?

If this aligns with the project's goals, I might be open to exploring the codebase further and perhaps drafting a PR for your review.

Thank you for your time!

issues.title: Metrics: Close HTTP connections when stopping the core
issues.body:
When an application embeds Xray and restarts an `Instance`, an HTTP collector can keep using its existing metrics keep-alive connection after `Instance.Close()`. The old handler remains available instead of the collector reconnecting to the new instance. This affects both direct `metrics.listen` and connections routed to `metrics.tag`.

`http.Serve` creates an HTTP server that the metrics handler does not retain. Closing its listeners stops new accepts, but leaves accepted connections open. Retain one `http.Server` for both listeners and close it with the metrics handler, while keeping the existing explicit listener cleanup. Capture the server before starting either serving goroutine so an immediate close is also handled.

The regression starts actual core instances, makes a successful HTTP/1.1 request, calls `Instance.Close`, then checks that the same connection can no longer receive any HTTP response. It covers `listen`, `tag`, and both together; all three fail against the original production code. Fixtures use only a loopback listener and in-memory connections.

Related: #6349, which supports restarting metrics-enabled instances in the same process.

issues.title: TUN inbound: Half-close the app connection when the outbound is done, instead of waiting for `uplinkOnly`
issues.body:
## Why

With Xray's TUN as the system VPN, an app that reads a response until the server closes waits about 1 s more than it should on every such connection. The outbound already knows the response is over, but TUN keeps the app's connection open until the whole dispatch ends, and that happens only after `uplinkOnly`. Examples are HTTP/1.0 without `Content-Length`, RTSP (Moonlight in #5845) and simple request and reply protocols. With this change the app gets the end of the response right away

## What changed

- TUN sends FIN to the app as soon as the outbound is done with the response. The app can still send, and the connection is closed as before when the dispatch is over
- the lightweight TCP stack gets `CloseWrite` for that
- the rest of the core still closes links in pairs, as agreed in the thread

## Testing and limits

- `TestTCPCloseWrite` checks that FIN goes out, that data from the app is still read after it and that `Close` sends nothing more. `go test -race ./proxy/tun` passes
- this helps only when the outbound itself sees the end of the response, for example freedom or VMess. Over VLESS the outbound ends only after `uplinkOnly` on the server, so the wait there stays

Related #5845 #7345

issues.title: TUN inbound: Route each new UDP destination, keeping FullCone NAT within a route
issues.body:
The UDP FullCone table (#5509) is keyed by the source only, and only the first packet of a session is routed, so later destinations of that source reuse its outbound. As the TUN never sees a socket close, a port that the OS reuses before the session expires inherits the old route. For example, DNS on a port last used by a direct or blocked flow never reaches the DNS outbound, and a resolver that retries from the same port (mDNSResponder) keeps the stale session alive.

Now a new destination is routed once, with fake IPs judged by their domain and no DNS lookup made. It then joins its source's session for the same rule, or gets a session of its own. Destinations of one rule still share a session, so FullCone is kept within a rule, and a balancer picking another outbound doesn't split it. Routing runs off the goroutine that reads the tun. WireGuard and MASQUE servers are unchanged.

Checked on a real utun on macOS with the system resolver: DNS on a reused port is answered and destinations of one rule leave from one port, while on main the DNS goes nowhere and every destination leaves from the first one. A new destination costs about 2 µs more; established flows and throughput are unchanged.

AI disclosure: this PR was completed using Claude Opus 5.5.

issues.title: GitHub Actions: Use Android packed relocations for Android builds
issues.body:
Android builds are PIE, and a Go PIE binary carries ~155k `R_*_RELATIVE` dynamic relocations (pointers in type descriptors, itabs, static string/slice headers, etc.). Stored as plain RELA (24 bytes each) they take **3.56 MiB** of every Android binary.

This PR passes `-Wl,--pack-dyn-relocs=android` to lld (NDK r28b, already used by the Android jobs), so the table is stored in Android's packed format (APS2) instead.

### Result (NDK r28b, same command line as `release.yml`)

| | before | after | diff |
|---|---|---|---|
| android-arm64-v8a | 36,447,032 B | 33,380,312 B | **−2.92 MiB (−8.4%)** |
| android-amd64 | 39,053,016 B | 35,980,920 B | **−2.93 MiB (−7.9%)** |
| relocation table (arm64) | 3,738,216 B (`RELA`) | 671,475 B (`ANDROID_RELA`) | |

The download (zip) shrinks less (~0.3 MiB) because RELA compresses well; the gain is mostly on-disk / installed size. Code and data are unchanged: only the encoding of the relocation table differs (e.g. `.data.rel.ro` has the same size in both builds).

### Compatibility

- `DT_ANDROID_RELA` is supported by the bionic loader since **Android 6.0 (API 23)**. The Android jobs already target API 24 (`*-linux-android24-clang`, "Android 7+" since #4664), so the supported range does not change.
- Binaries would fail to load on Android 5.x (API 21–22), which is already below the build target.
- RELR (`--pack-dyn-relocs=relr`) would save ~0.6 MiB more, but needs Android 9 (API 28, `DT_ANDROID_RELR`) or Android 11 (API 30, `DT_RELR`), so it is intentionally **not** used here.

### Testing

On a physical device (Android 16 / API 36, arm64), comparing the unchanged build with the packed one:

- `xray version`, `xray x25519`, `xray run -test`: OK
- end-to-end traffic inside the device: dokodemo-door → VLESS outbound → VLESS inbound → freedom → metrics HTTP endpoint: `200 OK`
- unit tests cross-compiled with the same flags and run on the device (`common/buf`, `common/crypto`, `common/protocol`, `common/serial`, `common/net`, `infra/conf`, `proxy/vless/encoding`, `app/router`): identical results for both builds, all PASS (geosite-dependent router tests skipped: no `geosite.dat` on the device)

Not tested on Android 6–8 hardware; compatibility there is based on the dynamic tags (`llvm-readelf -d` shows `ANDROID_RELA`/`ANDROID_RELASZ`) and bionic's documented support.

issues.title: XDRIVE transport: Add the Google Drive and "template" backend
issues.body:
This stacks on #6745. Until that one is merged the diff here also contains its commit.

### What it adds

A `Storage` implementation for Google Drive, selected with `"service": "Google Drive"`, where `remoteFolder` is a Drive folder id and `secrets` holds ClientID, ClientSecret and RefreshToken.

### No SDK

Plain `net/http`, zero new entries in `go.mod`. It sits behind the same five method `Storage` interface as the local backend, so another provider is one more file and still no dependency.

### How it works

Paths are flattened into single names, so `streams/abc/c2s/000000000.seg` becomes `streams~abc~c2s~000000000.seg`, because Drive has no cheap path lookup and creating nested folders would cost a request per level.

A name to id cache is filled from every listing, so a download costs one request instead of two. The access token is cached and refreshed on expiry or on a 401.

Requests are retried on 429 and 5xx with a jittered backoff capped at 2 seconds. Jitter matters here: at concurrency 32 every request hits the rate limit at the same moment, and synchronised retries only make it worse. A request whose context is already cancelled is not retried at all.

### Measurements

Both ends on a server in the Netherlands, against a real Google Drive account.

Raw storage:

* 4 sequential puts of 256 KiB: 199 KiB/s
* 8 parallel puts of 256 KiB: 1637 KiB/s
* 8 parallel gets of 256 KiB: 2453 KiB/s
* listing a folder of 13 objects: 250 ms
* an uploaded object becomes listable after about 200 ms, so the listing is fresh enough to drive the log

Transport, 10 MB pushed through the WAL:

* segment 128 KiB, concurrency 16: 1187 KiB/s
* segment 256 KiB, concurrency 16: 1513 KiB/s
* segment 256 KiB, concurrency 32: 1849 KiB/s
* segment 512 KiB, concurrency 32: 2111 KiB/s

Real proxy, curl through SOCKS into VLESS over XDRIVE over Google Drive:

* 50 MB in 21.6 s, 2258 KiB/s, about 18.5 Mbit/s, byte identical
* the first byte takes about 2 s, so bulk transfer is comfortable and interactive use is not

Mux, 30 parallel requests, which is roughly one web page:

* without mux: 23675 ms and 30 sessions
* with mux.cool at concurrency 8: 8605 ms and 4 sessions

Stability: 12 of 12 live runs against Drive.

### Tests

A fake Drive server on `httptest` covers upload, listing, download, delete, token caching and retries, and the whole transport is run over it. Live tests against a real account live in the same file and skip unless `XRAY_XDRIVE_DRIVE_SECRETS` points at a credentials file, so nothing here needs secrets in CI.

### Known limits

Credentials sit on the client, so this is for self hosted use. One outbound should enable mux.cool, otherwise every TCP connection becomes its own session with its own files. The HTTP client does not go through Xray's own dialer yet, so `sockopt` and a dialer proxy are not applied to Drive requests.

Feature Request: Dynamic uTLS Fingerprint Updates
issues.body:
Hello! Thanks for your great work on this project.

#### Problem
Censorship systems regularly block outdated TLS fingerprints (e.g., older versions of Chrome). Currently, the randomization algorithms still use these blocked fingerprints as a base for generating random ones, which leads to connection failures.

#### Proposed Solution
I suggest introducing a feature that allows updating the fingerprint bases independently of the main app source code updates. This could work similarly to how GeoIP and Geosite files are currently updated within the app.

#### Proposed Workflow
1. **Select Base:** The user selects a "Fingerprint Base" (e.g., Chrome).
2. **Update:** The user taps an "Update" button in a new menu (ideally placed next to the GeoIP/Geosite update options).
3. **Fetch:** client fetches the latest actual Chrome fingerprint from a remote, rolling-update repository.
4. **Generate:** The client build a new randomized fingerprint based on the freshly updated data from step 3.

#### UI Suggestion (uTLS Settings)
In the vless profile configuration, the uTLS settings could be structured as follows:

- **Chrome**
- **Firefox**
- *...*
- **Randomized**
  - Based on Chrome *(uses updated remote data)*
  - Based on Firefox *(uses updated remote data)*
  - *...*

This feature would significantly improve uTLS resilience against strict, adaptive censorship.

This way, GUI clients wouldn't need to deal with granular gRPC calls or rewrite their config generators — they could simply pass the newly generated `config.json` to the running `xray.exe` process without ever dropping the TUN interface or WFP protection. What are your thoughts on this?

comments.body:
Server side: agreed, closing the inbound connection unblocks it.

Client side does leak, though. If the connection drops during an upload, the session goroutines are blocked writing into the full 64 KiB uplink pipe. Nobody reads `uplinkReader` after `Process` returns, and `common.Interrupt(upLinkWriter)` no longer reaches the pipe, so they stay blocked for good (the rest wait on the `MutexWriter` lock behind them). This test fails on v26.11.9 and passes on v26.10.31 and with this PR:

<details><summary>test</summary>

```go
type dropOutbound chan struct{}

func (d dropOutbound) Process(context.Context, *transport.Link, internet.Dialer) error {
	<-d // never reads the uplink, then the connection "drops"
	return io.ErrUnexpectedEOF
}

func TestClientWorkerDropDuringUpload(t *testing.T) {
	drop := make(dropOutbound)
	w, _ := (&mux.DialingWorkerFactory{Proxy: drop, Strategy: mux.ClientStrategy{MaxConcurrency: 8, MaxConnection: 8}}).Create()
	ctx := session.ContextWithOutbounds(context.Background(), []*session.Outbound{{Target: net.TCPDestination(net.DomainAddress("example.com"), 80)}})
	r, wr := pipe.New(pipe.WithoutSizeLimit())
	_, out := pipe.New(pipe.WithoutSizeLimit())
	for i := 0; i < 32; i++ { // 256 KiB, more than the 64 KiB uplink pipe
		b := buf.New()
		b.Extend(buf.Size)
		wr.WriteMultiBuffer(buf.MultiBuffer{b})
	}
	w.Dispatch(ctx, &transport.Link{Reader: r, Writer: out})
	time.Sleep(500 * time.Millisecond)
	close(drop)
	<-w.WaitClosed()
	time.Sleep(time.Second)
	stack := make([]byte, 1<<20)
	if strings.Contains(string(stack[:runtime.Stack(stack, true)]), "mux.fetchInput") {
		t.Fatal("session goroutine still blocked on the uplink after the worker closed")
	}
}
```
</details>

issues.title: fix(xray): use a REALITY fingerprint the bundled Xray server accepts
issues.body:
Fixes #3413

## Problem

A new self-hosted XRay (VLESS + REALITY) server installed by the app does not pass traffic. The client shows "Connected", but every connection ends on the decoy site instead of going through the server.

## Root cause

- The client default fingerprint is `hellochrome_120` ([protocolConstants.h#L72](https://github.com/amnezia-vpn/amnezia-client/blob/ac175c8a8147cfe56f98c8372ec17ea2ba00bb02/client/core/utils/constants/protocolConstants.h#L72)).
- The server image installs Xray v26.10.31 ([Dockerfile#L4](https://github.com/amnezia-vpn/amnezia-client/blob/ac175c8a8147cfe56f98c8372ec17ea2ba00bb02/client/server_scripts/xray/Dockerfile#L4)). That release uses REALITY `83f621788ca8`, which contains XTLS/REALITY@8cdf7bf9c7f09cb9814bf08c3eb877f68b85fba8: a ClientHello without an `X25519MLKEM768` key share (placed before the optional `X25519` one) is no longer authenticated and is forwarded to the target as an ordinary visitor ([tls.go#L215-L236](https://github.com/XTLS/REALITY/blob/83f621788ca88b83179810b12baa7ae518aacb83/tls.go#L215-L236)).
- uTLS `HelloChrome_120` has no `X25519MLKEM768` share, so the server treats the client as a probe. The client then gets the target's real certificate, REALITY verification fails on every connection, and the Xray process itself keeps running, so the app still reports "Connected".
- The same check rejects several entries of the REALITY fingerprint list ([xrayConfigModel.cpp#L760-L763](https://github.com/amnezia-vpn/amnezia-client/blob/ac175c8a8147cfe56f98c8372ec17ea2ba00bb02/client/ui/models/protocols/xrayConfigModel.cpp#L760-L763)): `ios`, `android`, `edge`, `360`, `qq`, and `random` most of the time (it picks one of Xray's "modern" presets at start, several of which are older Chrome/iOS/Edge hellos).
- Configs created while `hellochrome_120` was the default keep it: in the stored server settings (`xray_fingerprint`), in the saved client config, and in keys/links exported from them.

## Fix

- `defaultFingerprint` is `chrome` again. Xray maps it to uTLS `HelloChrome_Auto`, which sends `X25519MLKEM768` and follows uTLS updates. Everything that falls back to the default picks this up: new installs (`InstallerBase`), `applyDefaults()`, client stream settings, imported links without `fp`, and export.
- The REALITY dropdown uses a new `realityFingerprintOptions()` = `chrome`, `firefox`, `safari`: the presets the bundled server accepts. The TLS dropdown keeps the full `fingerprintOptions()` list, because a plain TLS inbound accepts any ClientHello.
- Saved configs that still carry the old default are moved to the new one, for REALITY only:
  - `XrayServerConfig::fromJson()` replaces `hellochrome_120` with the default unless the security is `tls`, so the settings page and new exports use a working value;
  - `sanitizeNativeConfig()`, which already repairs the legacy `Mozilla/5.0` value on every connect (desktop and mobile), also replaces `hellochrome_120` in `realitySettings`. This fixes already issued `vpn://` keys on the receiving side without re-sharing.

  `hellochrome_120` cannot complete a REALITY handshake with any Xray server that has 8cdf7bf, while `chrome` works with both old and new servers (it also sends a plain `X25519` share), so the replacement cannot break a working connection. Other values a user picked on purpose (including `ios`, `edge` and so on) are left as they are; TLS settings are not touched.

## How tested

Sandboxed Linux containers, no network except loopback.

1. Real Xray handshake. Server: official Xray v26.10.31 (the version from the Dockerfile) with VLESS + REALITY + vision. Client: official Xray v26.7.28, which is what amnezia-xray-bindings 1.5.0 wraps (amnezia-xray-core v1.260728.0 has the same `transport/internet/tls/tls.go`, REALITY client and uTLS version). Decoy target: a local TLS 1.3 site. `curl --socks5-hostname` through the client to a local HTTP origin:

   | fingerprint | server v26.10.31 | server v26.7.28 |
   |---|---|---|
   | helloch

The same server/config works fine on other family members' devices (non-Linux),

- OS: Linux Mint 22.3 (x86_64)
- Client versions tested: 5.1.0.6 (ac175c8) and 5.0.3.0 (de93650) — same bug on both
- Protocol: AmneziaWG (container `amnezia-awg2`)
- Connection route mode: VpnOnlyForwardSites (site split tunneling also tested disabled — same result)
- Daemon binary: /opt/AmneziaVPN/bin/AmneziaVPN-service (systemd unit AmneziaVPN.service)

## Steps to reproduce
1. Open AmneziaVPN
2. Select server with AmneziaWG protocol
3. Click Connect
4. Connection drops after ~1 second

## What was already tried (no effect)
- Reinstalled the client (5.1.0.6 → 5.0.3.0)
- Removed server profile and re-added it with a freshly issued config
- Disabled site split tunneling completely
- Wiped user config (~/.config/AmneziaVPN.ORG)
- Restarted AmneziaVPN.service, rebooted the PC multiple times

## Actual result
Interface `amn0` is created, `amneziawg-go` starts, but peer configuration fails:
AmneziaVPN WireguardUtilsLinux : Created wireguard interface amn0
AmneziaVPN LinuxRouteMonitor : Adding exclusion route for /999999

AmneziaVPN WireguardGo : ERROR: (amn0) IPC error -22: failed to get peer by public key:

Note also the garbled peer key in the daemon log

while parsing the peer public key, which then leads to the malloc() crash.

## Expected result
AmneziaWG tunnel connects normally, as it does on other devices with the same server.

## Additional info
The issue is specific to AmneziaWG — the daemon crashes during peer setup, 
before any handshake, so this is not a network/provider block.

`LocalSocketController::activate()` compares the native list against the exact JSON array `["0.0.0.0/0", "::/0"]`. IPv4-only, reordered and duplicated defaults enter the custom-route branch, which bypasses the site allowlist. This comparison remains in `dev` at `3f6ecacff15e0ada890f6cf5174602d2b6b899c5`.

## Reproduction without changing a live VPN

I compiled the actual controller source and captured its activation message through an isolated QLocalServer/QLocalSocket pair. The test does not contact the real VPN service or alter routes.

Input with dummy endpoint information and no credentials:

```json
{
  "protocol": "awg",
  "awg_config_data": {
    "allowed_ips": ["0.0.0.0/0"],
    "hostName": "192.0.2.1"
  },
  "splitTunnelType": 1,
  "splitTunnelSites": ["198.51.100.0/24", "203.0.113.7"]
}
```

Also reproducible with `protocol: "wireguard"` and `wireguard_config_data`.

**Actual activation message:**

```json
"allowedIPAddressRanges": [
  {"address": "0.0.0.0", "range": 0, "isIpv6": false}
]
```

**Expected:**

```json
"allowedIPAddressRanges": [
  {"address": "198.51.100.0", "range": 24, "isIpv6": false},
  {"address": "203.0.113.7", "range": 32, "isIpv6": false}
]
```

Using `["::/0", "0.0.0.0/0"]` also incorrectly selects the native/full-tunnel branch. IPv6 entries in that branch additionally receive `isIpv6: false`.

## Environment and verification limits

- Windows x64, Qt 6.10.1, MSVC 19.53.
- Reproduced against the source used by my local 5.0.3.2 build, based on upstream 5.0.3.1. The relevant comparison remains unchanged in current dev.
- This establishes the generated daemon configuration; I have **not** switched my live VPN to allowlist mode for an end-to-end traffic test.
- A focused regression suite covers both protocols, all site route modes, native profile variants and application-exclusion passthrough: **26 failures before the fix, 0 afterwards**, across 60 data cases plus setup/cleanup.

## Proposed fix and related work

Honor the site allowlist whenever the profile permits the IPv4 default route, independently of IPv6 presence, order or duplicates. Preserve restricted native AllowedIPs; normalize serialized prefixes, retain the correct address family and deduplicate routes.

The fix and regression tests are now isolated in #3379 ([01f19433](https://github.com/makkoar/amnezia-client/commit/01f1943324171e8be1eaca7f7f150c0897681b74)), extracted from the former combined #3030. The standalone branch is based directly on dev at `3f6ecacf`; rerunning the suite still gives 26 failures before and none after. Umbrella tracker: #3378. The other parts are #3380 / #3376 (hostnames and DNS) and #3030 / #3377 (Windows route application). There is overlap with #3011, which already addresses the IPv4-only allowlist branch; #3097 addresses the earlier eligibility check. #2907 and #3314 report related macOS symptoms, but this reproduction does not establish that all their observations share the same cause.

This concerns **site** split tunneling, not application allowlist support on Windows.

**Describe the bug**

On Kubuntu 24.04 with AmneziaVPN 5.0.1.5 and AmneziaWG, automatic VPN connection after system boot may fail.

Amnezia creates the `amn0` interface and installs the default split routes:

0.0.0.0/1 dev amn0 metric 1
128.0.0.0/1 dev amn0 metric 1

However, during the failed autoconnect attempt, the exclusion route to the VPN server endpoint is not created.

The log contains:

getGatewayAndIface: no gateway found
No default gateway available, skipping exclusion route

After that, Amnezia tries to establish the AmneziaWG connection, but the handshake cannot be completed and the client remains in the "Connecting" state indefinitely.

The log also contains:

Failed to send handshake initiation: network is unreachable

At this point there is no Internet connectivity.

If I manually click Disconnect and then Connect in the AmneziaVPN GUI, the connection succeeds immediately.

During the successful manual connection Amnezia correctly detects the physical gateway and creates the exclusion route:

Adding exclusion route for <VPN_SERVER_IP>/32
Gateway 192.168.1.1 for interface wlp0s20f3

After that the VPN and Internet connection work normally.


**To Reproduce**

1. Configure AmneziaVPN to automatically connect using AmneziaWG.
2. Reboot Kubuntu.
3. Log in and wait for AmneziaVPN autoconnect.
4. AmneziaVPN remains in the connecting state and Internet access is unavailable.
5. Check the routing table. The following routes exist:

0.0.0.0/1 dev amn0 metric 1
128.0.0.0/1 dev amn0 metric 1

but there is no host route for the VPN endpoint via the physical Wi-Fi gateway.
6. In AmneziaVPN manually click Disconnect.
7. Click Connect.
8. The VPN connects successfully and Internet access is restored.
9. The routing table now contains an exclusion route similar to:

<VPN_SERVER_IP> via 192.168.1.1 dev wlp0s20f3


**Expected behavior**

AmneziaVPN should not install routes that direct the VPN server endpoint itself into `amn0`.

Before redirecting traffic through `amn0`, the client should ensure that an exclusion route to the VPN endpoint through the physical network gateway exists.

If the default gateway is not yet available during autoconnect, AmneziaVPN should wait/retry instead of continuing with a configuration in which the VPN endpoint becomes unreachable.

I tried adding the following systemd dependency to `AmneziaVPN.service`:

[Unit]
Wants=network-online.target
After=network-online.target

`NetworkManager-wait-online.service` is enabled and completes successfully.

After adding this route, I rebooted the system again.

This suggests that the problem is related to a race condition / missing exclusion route for the VPN endpoint during autoconnect.


**Log files**

A sanitized log showing the failed automatic connection followed by a successful manual Disconnect -> Connect can be provided/attached.

The real VPN server IP address has been replaced with `<VPN_SERVER_IP>`.

- Connection: Wi-Fi
- AmneziaVPN version: 5.0.1.5
- Protocol: AmneziaWG

issues.title: fix: use packet-up xhttp mode in the network extension
issues.body:
FIX importat IOS network extension break down.
On iOS the network extension was jetsam-killed at the 50 MB limit a few minutes
after connecting to an xhttp + REALITY server (`The VPN plugin died unexpectedly`).

With `mode` unset xray picks `stream-one` for xhttp + REALITY: one endless POST
per session, and Go's HTTP/2 client holds a 512 KiB scratch buffer per such
stream for its whole lifetime. A heap profile from the extension showed
`http2.(*clientStream).writeRequestBody` at 34.5 MB (74 % of the Go heap) with
~70 sessions, which Instagram/Facebook open within a minute.

The extension now sets `xhttpSettings.mode = "packet-up"` when the mode is empty
or `auto`: each POST has a `Content-Length`, so the buffer is payload-sized and
transient. An explicit mode is left as is; the server accepts both modes.
iOS extension only.

issues.title: [Obsolete following the release of AWG 3.0] Static I1 junk-packet value in default/self-host configs creates a cross-deployment DPI fingerprint
issues.body:
The self-hosted AmneziaWG 2.0 setup docs/installer ship a hardcoded value for I1 (first special junk packet):
I1 = <r 2><b 0x858000010001000000000669636c6f756403636f6d0000010001c00c000100010000105a00044d583737>
Decoding the payload shows it is a well-formed DNS response for icloud.com (flags 0x8580 = QR=1, AA, RD, RA; A record, TTL 0x105a, IP 77.88.55.55 encoded in the last 4 bytes). This is not a randomized template — it is byte-identical across any deployment where the operator copy-pasted the documented example (which, anecdotally, appears to be common practice, since this is the value given directly in the official self-host guide).
Why this matters
The entire point of I1–I5 / protocol mimicry is that AmneziaWG traffic should be indistinguishable from real background protocol traffic on a per-deployment basis, just like H1–H4 are deliberately randomized ranges that must not overlap between installs. A static, publicly-documented junk packet defeats this:
	1.	Global signature, not per-deployment: Any DPI system that captures this exact 44-byte UDP payload once can build a static signature valid for every AmneziaWG self-host instance that used the documented default — not just one server. This is categorically worse than a fixed H1–H4, since those are at least opaque integers with no fixed semantic payload; I1 here is a complete, parseable, byte-exact DNS message.
	2.	Correlation/detection before handshake analysis: An observer doesn’t need to fingerprint the WireGuard handshake shape at all — matching this one packet on a UDP port is sufficient to flag “this is likely AmneziaWG,” independent of the H1–H4 randomization that the rest of the protocol relies on.
	3.	Low-risk-of-edits problem: Because I1 requires exact byte-perfect DNS structure (correct section counts/lengths per the <r N><b 0x...> format), users are unlikely to manually randomize it themselves — a single miscounted byte produces a malformed DNS packet, which is arguably a stronger detection signal (a broken protocol pretending to be a normal one) than leaving it static. In practice this discourages exactly the mitigation that would fix the issue.
Suggested fix
	•	Installer/config generator should auto-generate I1 (and I2–I5, if used) per-deployment: a syntactically valid DNS query/response for a randomly chosen, plausible domain, with randomized transaction ID / TTL / answer IP where applicable, rather than shipping one canonical example.
	•	Update the self-host documentation so the sample I1 value is clearly marked as illustrative-only (“do not use verbatim in production”), or better, replace the doc example with a small script/tool that generates a valid signature automatically (the existing Wireshark-based manual guide is good for custom protocols but too error-prone/tedious to expect users to do it for the common DNS case).
	•	Consider validating at parse time that I1–I5 differ from the documented example value(s), and warn the user if they match.

On macOS this fails with `Failed to set IPv4: Destination address required`. Resolved IPv6 server addresses are also assigned to IPv4 fields, and the macOS backend emits an unbracketed IPv6 endpoint, failing with IPC error -22.

The iOS/macOS Network Extension has a separate config serializer which also emits IPv6 endpoints without brackets, causing WireGuardKit to reject the generated config before starting the tunnel.

This change:
- Separates interface addresses by family before constructing desktop daemon requests, preserving an explicit IPv6 address and retaining the existing fallback for IPv4-only profiles.
- Assigns resolved server addresses and gateways to the correct address-family fields for macOS, Windows and Linux.
- Formats IPv6 endpoints with brackets in the macOS backend, shared config export, and the iOS/macOS Network Extension serializer.
- Permits only UDP to the configured IPv6 server address and port through the macOS/Linux kill switch, retaining the default IPv6 block. Linux replaces stale endpoint exceptions while keeping a blocking rule installed.
- Adds C++ regression tests and Apple serialization tests using the real WireGuardKit endpoint parser.

Validation:
- 18 Qt Test checks passed, including dual-stack address order, invalid/duplicate addresses, IPv4, IPv6, scoped IPv6, NAT64 and hostname endpoints, plus narrow IPv6 firewall exceptions and invalid endpoint/port rejection.
- 10 Apple config combinations passed (IPv4, IPv6, already bracketed IPv6, NAT64, hostname; IPv4-only and dual-stack interface addresses). The parser also rejects the original malformed IPv6 endpoint.
- Changed Swift sources type-checked against the iPhoneOS SDK for arm64.
- Windows/Linux endpoint and interface consumers were reviewed: they already support separate address-family fields, and now receive them correctly from the shared controller. The changed Linux firewall translation unit also compiled with Qt on macOS; native Linux integration was not run.
- Android was reviewed: it already splits interface addresses and brackets IPv6 endpoints, so no Android change is needed.
- Full macOS arm64 application, daemon and test targets built successfully.
- Full CTest run: 32/33 suites passed. OpenSSLLibraryTest fails its Qt/app version equality assertion because Homebrew Qt uses OpenSSL 4 while Conan dependencies use OpenSSL 3. A separate HTTPS probe linking the same Qt and Conan libraries completed TLS verification and returned HTTP 200.
- Installed the macOS app and updated privileged service, then verified a real connection using a hostname resolving to IPv6 with the kill switch enabled. The UI reports Connected, the separate CLI tunnel is stopped, the default IPv4 route uses the app tunnel, and an HTTPS request through it returned HTTP 200.
- Ordinary IPv6 Internet traffic remains blocked by the existing kill-switch policy; the new exception is limited to the VPN transport.
- Windows/Linux/Android application builds and a real-device iOS connection have not been run locally.

Fixes #1630.

comments.issue_title: WFP/Split Tunneling breaks when IP Forwarding and Hyper-V Internal Switch are enabled
comments.body:
I found a working configuration workaround on my machine. No driver changes were required.

**Original setup:** Ethernet uplink, AmneziaWG, Brave excluded by application, site-based split tunneling disabled. Enabling Windows Mobile Hotspot broke connectivity in Brave.

### What worked

1. Changed Windows Internet Connection Sharing to share the **AmneziaVPN adapter** with the Wi-Fi Direct hotspot adapter, instead of sharing Ethernet.
2. After this change, Brave could connect directly through Ethernet, but the phone initially had no Internet access.
3. Added an on-link host route for the phone’s static address (`192.168.137.201/32`) through the hotspot adapter.

The route needed special handling: Amnezia’s `WindowsRouteMonitor` also cloned the initial host route into the VPN interface, causing return traffic to the phone to take the wrong interface.

Setting the hotspot host route’s metric to `0x5e72` (24178), the existing `EXCLUSION_ROUTE_METRIC` value recognized by the route monitor, prevented that route from being cloned. I also removed the VPN `/32` clone created during testing.

A small local helper now maintains this single host route and starts at Windows sign-in.

### Verified

- Excluded Brave connects directly through Ethernet.
- Ordinary VPN traffic continues through the VPN.
- The phone has Internet access through the shared VPN, with cellular data disabled.
- Both Brave and the phone still work after reconnecting the VPN and after toggling Mobile Hotspot.

A full Windows reboot has not yet been tested.

### Limitations

This is a **workaround**, not a fix for the original driver/ICS interaction. It depends on an internal route-metric marker and the phone’s fixed IP address, so it should not be treated as a general solution.

It also changes the phone’s Internet path: the phone now uses the shared VPN.

comments.issue_title: Linux: IPv6 endpoint not bracketed before wireguard-go IPC, peer creation fails with IPC error -22
comments.body:
Reproduced on AmneziaVPN **5.1.0.6** (Linux Mint 22.3, userspace `amneziawg-go`, kernel has no AmneziaWG module) with an **IPv6-only** endpoint: the host name has an AAAA record and **no A record at all**, so there is no IPv4 fallback path. Same symptom as reported here, plus a second defect that blocks the connection even after this one is fixed.

## 1. The endpoint is handed to wireguard-go without brackets (this issue)

```
[DEBUG] WireguardUtilsLinux : Configuring peer <key> via 2001:db8:1234:5678::
[DEBUG] WireguardGo : ERROR: (amn0) IPC error -22: failed to set endpoint 2001:db8:1234:5678:::443:
        invalid ip:port "2001:db8:1234:5678:::443", IPv6 addresses must be surrounded by square brackets
[ERROR] DaemonLocalServerConnection : Failed to activate the interface
```

The literal travels through the **IPv4** branch of `client/platforms/linux/daemon/wireguardutilslinux.cpp` (`updatePeer()`), so the branch that adds brackets never runs:

```cpp
if (!config.m_serverIpv4AddrIn.isNull()) {
    out << "endpoint=" << config.m_serverIpv4AddrIn << ":";      // ← takes the IPv6 literal, no brackets
} else if (!config.m_serverIpv6AddrIn.isNull()) {
    out << "endpoint=[" << config.m_serverIpv6AddrIn << "]:";
}
out << config.m_serverPort << "\n";
```

`m_serverIpv4AddrIn` is filled from `serverIpv4AddrIn` in `client/daemon/daemon.cpp`, which is where the resolved address ends up regardless of its family. `client/daemon/interfaceconfig.cpp` (`toWgConf`) has the same shape, with the IPv6 `Endpoint` line commented out. The error text itself comes from Go's `net/netip` (`netip.ParseAddrPort`, called from `amneziawg-go`'s `conn.StdNetBind.ParseEndpoint`), which deliberately refuses to guess where the address ends and the port begins.

Minimal fix that needs no guessing — bracket by content, in the same `if`:

```cpp
const QString addr = config.m_serverIpv4AddrIn;
out << "endpoint=" << (addr.contains(':') ? "[" + addr + "]" : addr) << ":";
```

(or keep the families apart where the config is populated, then the existing IPv6 branch works as written).

## 2. Separate defect: no exclusion route is created for an IPv6 endpoint

With (1) fixed the peer is created, routes are installed — and the handshake still cannot complete, because the endpoint ends up inside the tunnel:

```
[DEBUG] LinuxRouteMonitor : Adding exclusion route for 2001:db8:1234:5678::/128
[WARNING] LinuxRouteMonitor : No default gateway available, skipping exclusion route
[DEBUG] LinuxRouteMonitor : Adding route to ::/1
[DEBUG] LinuxRouteMonitor : Adding route to 8000::/1
[DEBUG] Daemon : Checking for handshake...
[DEBUG] DaemonLocalServerConnection : Command received: deactivate        # ~13 s later, no handshake
```

`::/1` + `8000::/1` cover the endpoint as well, so the handshake packets are sent into the tunnel that is still down. On the same host the IPv4 default gateway exists and IPv4 exclusions work (we keep a `/32` route for the server address), so this looks like an IPv6 gap in the gateway lookup, not a missing route. Adding `2001:db8:1234:5678::/128 via <current IPv6 default gateway> dev <iface>` by hand makes the handshake go through immediately.

## Workaround we run meanwhile

Patched `amneziawg-go`'s `conn.StdNetBind.ParseEndpoint` to also accept a bare `addr:port` form (port separated by the last colon, remainder must parse as an IPv6 address) — that removes the `IPC error -22` — plus the manual `/128` exclusion route. With those two the tunnel comes up and carries traffic. Both fixes are on our side only; the report is about the client.

Full logs (`-u AmneziaVPN.service`) available on request.

comments.issue_title: Linux 5.0.1.5: exclusion routes never installed — netlink route dump overflows the   fixed 8 KiB buffer
comments.body:
Today I have met this issue too, trying to install huge list of sites (> 9k) to exclude from vpn.
Two things not covered above, both specific to "All sites except listed" split tunneling. Reproduced on 5.1.0.6.

### 1. A long site list overflows the buffer by itself, and both open PRs only move the cutoff.
`rtmSendRoute()` calls `getGatewayAndIface()` once per exclusion route, and every route it installs adds 60 bytes to the next dump. So the list fills the buffer partway through the connect, even on a host with a small routing table. 

| Receive buffer | Exclusions installed |
|---|---|
| 8 KiB (current) | 115 |
| 64 KiB (size used in #3231) | 1,071 |
| 128 KiB (size used in #3170) | 2,163 |
| Parse each datagram, stop at the default route | all installed |

So a fix needs either a parser that never accumulates the whole dump, or the gateway resolved once per `activate()`/`switchServer()` and passed down.

### 2. Disconnect can't remove the routes.
`deleteExclusionRoute()` takes the same `RTN_THROW` branch, so it does the same lookup. At disconnect the table is still over the limit, so every delete is skipped and all installed exclusions stay in the main table (in the netns test, 0 of 115 were removed). The next connect then can't add any exclusion, the endpoint route included. Deleting shouldn't need the lookup at all: the kernel deletes the route by prefix without a gateway.

- The same HAPP configuration worked on an Android phone connected to the same Wi-Fi network.
- Reinstalling VPN clients, rebooting Windows, resetting routes and Winsock did not solve the problem.
- Disabling the Kaspersky NDIS network filter did not change anything.

## Diagnosis

The issue was related to Windows routing when a VPN TUN interface was active.

When HAPP started, it created a virtual network interface and installed a default route (`0.0.0.0/0`) through that interface.

As a result, Windows could also select the VPN tunnel as the route for packets addressed to the VPN server itself.

This creates a routing/bootstrap loop: the VPN client needs to reach its remote server through the physical network interface before the tunnel can work, but Windows may attempt to send that connection through the tunnel being established.

The issue was identified using PowerShell:

```powershell
Find-NetRoute -RemoteIPAddress <VPN_SERVER_IP> |
Format-List InterfaceAlias, InterfaceIndex, DestinationPrefix, NextHop
```

When the result showed the virtual VPN interface instead of the physical network adapter, it indicated incorrect route selection.

## Workaround: Add an explicit host route for each VPN server

The solution was to add a `/32` host route for each VPN server endpoint, forcing Windows to reach that endpoint directly through the physical network interface.

### 1. Identify the physical network interface and gateway

For Android USB tethering:

```powershell
Get-NetIPConfiguration |
Where-Object {$_.IPv4DefaultGateway} |
Format-Table InterfaceAlias, InterfaceIndex,
@{N='IP';E={$_.IPv4Address.IPAddress -join ','}},
@{N='Gateway';E={$_.IPv4DefaultGateway.NextHop -join ','}} -AutoSize
```

Important: use the actual gateway address, not the computer's own IP address.

### 2. Add a route for the VPN server

Run PowerShell as Administrator:

```powershell
New-NetRoute `
-DestinationPrefix "<VPN_SERVER_IP>/32" `
-InterfaceIndex <PHYSICAL_INTERFACE_INDEX> `
-NextHop "<PHYSICAL_GATEWAY_IP>" `
-RouteMetric 1 `
-PolicyStore ActiveStore
```

For example, use the interface index and gateway belonging to the currently active Wi-Fi or USB RNDIS connection.

### 3. Verify the route

```powershell
Find-NetRoute -RemoteIPAddress <VPN_SERVER_IP> |
Format-List InterfaceAlias, InterfaceIndex, DestinationPrefix, NextHop
```

The result should point to the physical network adapter (Wi-Fi or USB RNDIS), NOT the VPN TUN interface.

### 4. Repeat for other VPN endpoints

Each VPN client may connect to a different server IP.

In my case:
- Adding a host route for the HAPP/Xray server through the physical Wi-Fi gateway restored HAPP connectivity.
- Adding a separate host route for the AmneziaWG server through the Android USB RNDIS gateway restored AmneziaWG connectivity.

The routes must use the gateway and interface of the currently active physical connection.

## Important notes

- Do not use the computer's own interface IP as `NextHop`. Use `IPv4DefaultGateway.NextHop`.
- Do not assume that all VPN clients use the same server IP.
- HAPP may use automatic server selection or multiple remote endpoints. Check the actual remote IP addresses used by Xray.

issues.title: feat(acl): switch ACL engine to expr
issues.body:
Replaces the ACL engine with one based on [expr](https://expr-lang.org/), so rules can match on more than the destination. The main use case is routing by authentication ID:

```yaml
acl:
  rules:
    - outbound: alice_exit
      match: auth.id == "alice"
    - outbound: reject
      match: geoip("cn") || cidr("10.0.0.0/8", client.ip)
    - outbound: default
      match: dst.port == 53 && cidr("8.8.8.8")
      hijack: 1.1.1.1
    - legacy: reject(geosite:category-ads-all)
    - legacyFile: /etc/hysteria/acl.txt
    - outbound: direct
```

- New `acl.rules` / `acl.rulesFile` (YAML list). Rules see `proto`, `dst.{host,port,ipv4,ipv6}`, `auth.id` and `client.{ip,port}`, plus `domain`, `suffix`, `cidr`, `geoip`, `geosite` and `legacy` matchers. Called with one argument they match the destination like before; with two, an explicit value (e.g. `client.ip`). Typos, non-boolean rules and unknown GeoIP/GeoSite names fail at load time
- Legacy `acl.file` / `acl.inline` keep working and are translated to expr internally. Legacy lines can also be mixed into `acl.rules` via `legacy` / `legacyFile` entries, so you can add a rule above an existing list without converting it
- `hysteria acl translate` prints the legacy rules as `acl.rules` YAML; `hysteria acl test -c server.yaml [--auth ID] [--client IP] [--proto udp] host:port` shows which rule and outbound a request would use, without connecting
- The match cache key only includes auth ID / client address when a rule uses them, so legacy rulesets cache exactly as before

**Breaking changes**
- `server.Outbound` methods now take a `*server.RequestInfo` (auth ID and client address) as the first argument. This affects programs that embed core
- Legacy port ranges starting at 0 (e.g. `udp/0-100`, `tcp/0`) used to match every port; they now match only the given range

**Performance** (100 rules, no GeoIP/GeoSite)

| | Old engine | New engine |
|---|---|---|
| Cache hit | 184 ns | 114 ns |
| Cache miss (no rule matches) | 2.9 µs | 8.4 µs |

Misses cost about 3× more because expr allocates an argument list per function call. A miss happens once per new destination (up to the 1024-entry cache), and is small next to the DNS lookup every request already does when ACL is enabled. Hits are faster because the cache key is now a struct instead of a formatted string.

**Testing**
- Every existing compile test runs against both the old compiler (kept in a test file for now) and the translated rules. A comparison test checks 30 legacy rule types against ~700 requests and requires identical results except the port-0 fix. A fuzzer found no mismatches in ~850k inputs
- Integration test checks the auth ID and client address reach the outbound for TCP, the first UDP packet, and later UDP destinations
- End to end with two users: the same destination is rejected for one and allowed for the other
